# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles spatial coordinates, spatial-scope tags and post-colonial population series for 838 individually assessed settlements across Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Mozambique and six neighbouring border buffers between 1964AD and 2025AD. Screened from 897 candidate municipal records and satellite-delineated urban agglomerations (59 duplicate aliases excluded), the retained ledger spans 3.300 chronological observations partitioned into 828 city-proper settlements and 10 metropolitan agglomerations. Active interpolated settlements expand from 72 entries in 1964AD to 124 in 1983AD, 325 in 2002AD and 694 in 2025AD, documenting urban growth from Copperbelt mining towns and colonial administrative hubs to multi-million agglomerations at Lubumbashi (3,92M), Lusaka (3,23M), Maputo (2,98M), Harare (2,92M), Lilongwe (1,38M) and Blantyre (1,31M).



# Background

Post-colonial urban hierarchies across Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi and Mozambique reflect markedly different colonial baselines, resource endowments and post-independence policies [@Bank2022ZambiaUrbanization; @Bank2021MozambiqueNorthern]. Zambia entered independence in 1964AD with an unusually urbanised mining belt alongside a sparsely populated interior, before shifting administrative and demographic weight toward Lusaka after the 1975AD copper downturn [@ZamStats2023ZambiaCensus; @Wotela2025UsingCensus]. Zimbabwe combined industrial Highveld corridors anchored by Harare and Bulawayo with late-colonial mobility restrictions that yielded rapid peri-urban growth in Chitungwiza and Epworth after 1980AD [@ZIMSTAT2023ZimbabweCensus; @Muzondi2014UrbanizationAnd]. Malawi sustained extreme rural smallholder density across its Shire Highlands and Central plains while relocating its national capital from Zomba to Lilongwe [@NSOMalawi2019Census; @Maviko2025ImpactSustainable]. Mozambique endured civil war disruption between 1977AD and 1992AD before rapid coastal and northern urban expansion in Maputo-Matola, Beira, Nampula, Pemba and Montepuez [@INEMozambique2019RGPH; @Mottelson2023UrbanDensity; @Shannon2018SustainableUrbanization].

# Methodology

## Candidate Screening and Territorial Accounting

Candidate entries were compiled from national census tables published by ZamStats, ZIMSTAT, the National Statistical Office of Malawi and INE Mozambique, supplemented by late-colonial enumerations and satellite-delineated urban agglomeration polygons [@ZamStats2023ZambiaCensus; @ZIMSTAT2023ZimbabweCensus; @NSOMalawi2019Census; @INEMozambique2019RGPH; @Wagenaar2018DevelopingRepresentative]. Out of 897 candidate entries inside and adjacent to the 2.015.507 km² study perimeter bounded on geoBoundaries outlines [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries], 59 duplicate alias or overlapping district records were excluded, retaining 838 settlements across 3.300 observations. Of those, 762 entries fall inside the 33 first-level administrative sub-regions while 76 sit in contiguous border-buffer corridors across six neighbouring countries.

## Scope Classification and Benchmark Interpolation

Each record carries an explicit spatial scope distinguishing 828 city-proper municipalities from 10 metropolitan agglomerations so core cities and adjacent dormitory municipalities such as Maputo and Matola or Harare, Chitungwiza and Epworth remain traceable without double counting [@Jorge2014ProcessosDinamicas; @Muzondi2014UrbanizationAnd; @Biza2025SanitaryCivility]. Country tables below report linearly interpolated populations across six decennial-scale benchmarks (1970AD, 1980AD, 1990AD, 2000AD, 2010AD and 2025AD) alongside each settlement's observed peak population and year, marking eras prior to or beyond observed records with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across all 838 entries, ordinary least-squares rank-size regression on peak populations returns $q = 1,04$ ($R^2 = 0,98$) over the upper fitted sample (n=180) and $q = 1,06$ ($R^2 = 0,97$) across the full ledger. Figure \ref{fig:settlements-rank} displays the 766 spatially deduplicated settlements ($q = 0,98$, $R^2 = 0,99$) alongside 2025AD sub-regional densities, confirming close alignment between urban agglomeration counts and national census distributions [@Bank2022ZambiaUrbanization; @Bank2021MozambiqueNorthern].

## Zambia Urban Hierarchy

## Zimbabwe Urban Hierarchy

Table \ref{tab:sett-zimbabwe} catalogues all 86 Zimbabwean settlements, tracing the Harare agglomeration (2,92M) alongside municipal Harare (1,49M), Bulawayo (676,7k peak), Chitungwiza (371,2k), Mutare (224,8k), Epworth (206,4k) and Gweru (159,1k) [@ZIMSTAT2023ZimbabweCensus; @Muzondi2014UrbanizationAnd; @NMMZ2022ZimbabweSites].

# Limitations

Three caveats govern this settlement ledger. First, 128 of the 838 entries carry single-date observations, primarily newly threshold-crossing peri-urban agglomerations recorded only in 2020AD-2025AD satellite grids; benchmark columns outside their observed span appear as a hyphen (-). Second, municipal census boundaries frozen over time separate city-proper cores from extra-municipal satellites such as Matola, Chitungwiza and Epworth, meaning both individual municipal rows and metropolitan agglomerations must be consulted together [@Jorge2014ProcessosDinamicas; @Muzondi2014UrbanizationAnd]. Third, wartime census interruption in Mozambique between 1980AD and 1997AD and recent Cabo Delgado displacement leave intercensal urban series reliant on satellite-assisted demographic reconciliation [@Wagenaar2018DevelopingRepresentative; @Bank2021MozambiqueNorthern].

# Conclusion

Taken together, the 838 individually assessed settlements trace six decades of post-colonial urban restructuring across Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Mozambique and their borderlands, documenting the pivot from colonial mining and railway towns toward multi-million capital agglomerations, secondary regional ports and dense peri-urban corridors.
